title: Southern Italy
subtitle: Campania, Puglia and Basilicata
objectives: Describe the main wines of Campania
Explain why volcanic soils matter in the south

steps.title: Campania
steps.body: Campania, around Naples, grows ancient grapes. Aglianico makes Taurasi, a powerful, tannic red often called the Barolo of the south. Fiano di Avellino and Greco di Tufo are DOCG whites, nutty and mineral. Vesuvius and the inland hills have volcanic soils, which drain well and resisted phylloxera in places.

steps.title: Puglia and Basilicata
steps.body: Puglia, the heel of Italy, is hot, flat and productive. Primitivo, the same grape as Zinfandel, gives ripe, high-alcohol reds, especially in Manduria. Negroamaro makes reds and rosés in Salento. In Basilicata, Aglianico del Vulture grows on the slopes of an extinct volcano, at up to 800 m, giving fresher Aglianico.

steps.explanation: Taurasi is Campania's DOCG Aglianico, structured and long-lived.

steps.title: Heat and altitude
steps.body: The south is hot, so the best wines come from altitude, sea breezes or volcanic slopes. Irpinia's vineyards, for Taurasi and Fiano, reach 400 to 700 m. Volcanic soils also give a distinctive savoury, smoky edge, and often ungrafted old vines.
steps.highlight: Altitude and volcanoes temper the heat

steps.explanation: Primitivo di Manduria comes from Puglia.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Campania's Aglianico makes Taurasi; Fiano and Greco are its whites
Altitude and volcanic soils give freshness in the hot south
